title: Divers Find What May Be the World’s Oldest Shipwreck
paragraphs: A shipwreck lying in shallow water off Kekova, west of Antalya, may be the oldest ever identified, according to a team of archaeologists who date it to about 2700–2400 BCE, roughly 4,500 years ago. If the dating holds, it would overtake a wreck off Dokos in Greece, estimated at 4,200 years, by some three centuries.

Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University located the site in 2024, following up on hints from local seafarers. The ship’s timbers have long since vanished; what is left is its cargo of large storage jars, many with a raised clay belt, wedged into a rocky underwater slope. Divers needed about four months to prise the pottery free of barnacles. A preliminary assessment suggests that some jars, or the clay they were made from, came from the Central Jordan Valley. Macquarie University’s Karin Sowada, who helped date the pottery, describes such remains as “a time capsule of ancient trade.”

Several caveats apply. The findings have not been peer reviewed, the dating is provisional, and the chemistry of the residue inside the jars, which might point to olive oil, wine or tree resin, is still being analysed. The vessel’s direction of travel is unknown, and the authors speculate that it sank while seeking shelter from a storm.

questions.q: What would the wreck overtake as the oldest known?
questions.a: The wreck off Dokos in Greece, about 4,200 years old.

questions.q: What survives of the ship itself?
questions.a: Only its cargo of storage jars; the timbers have gone.

questions.q: Which parts of the story are still uncertain?
questions.a: The date, the contents and origin of the jars, and the ship’s route.
